question_html: Under section 23(1), through which of the following modes may a public company issue securities?

options.A: To the public through a prospectus (public offer), or through private placement complying with section 42, or through a rights issue or bonus issue in accordance with the Act (and, if listed or proposed to be listed, also the SEBI Act, 1992 and regulations made thereunder)
options.B: Only through a public offer by way of prospectus, private placement and rights/bonus issues being permitted exclusively to private companies
options.C: Only through private placement, since a public company is statutorily barred from making any public offer of securities
options.D: Only through a rights issue, since bonus issues and private placement are available exclusively to private companies

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) To the public through a prospectus (public offer), or through private placement complying with section 42, or through a rights issue or bonus issue in accordance with the Act (and, if listed or proposed to be listed, also the SEBI Act, 1992 and regulations made thereunder)

Section 23(1) permits a public company to issue securities: (a) to the public through a prospectus (public offer), by complying with sections 23-41; or (b) through private placement under section 42; or (c) through a rights issue or bonus issue, additionally complying with SEBI Act provisions where the company is listed or proposes to be listed.

options.A: A private company may issue securities through a public offer by prospectus in the same manner as a public company, subject only to a higher minimum subscription threshold

options.A: Public offer refers exclusively to an initial public offer (IPO), with a further public offer and an offer for sale being treated as private placements under the Act
options.B: Public offer includes only an offer for sale (OFS) by an existing shareholder, an IPO and FPO being treated as forms of private placement

question_html: Which of the following instruments is expressly excluded from the definition of 'securities' as adopted by section 2(81) of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Government securities
options.B: Derivatives
options.C: Units or any other instrument issued by any collective investment scheme to investors in such schemes
options.D: A unit linked insurance policy (ULIP) issued by an insurer, which provides a combined benefit of risk cover on life and investment

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) A unit linked insurance policy (ULIP) issued by an insurer, which provides a combined benefit of risk cover on life and investment

Section 2(81) adopts the definition of 'securities' in section 2(h) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, which includes shares, derivatives, collective investment scheme units, security receipts, mutual fund units, government securities, and rights/interests in securities - but expressly excludes a unit linked insurance policy or similar combined risk-and-investment instrument issued by an insurer under the Insurance Act, 1938.

question_html: Which of the following matters is administered by the Central Government, Tribunal, or Registrar (and not by SEBI), even in the case of a listed company?

options.A: Issue of securities by a listed company to the public
options.B: Redemption of preference shares
options.C: Transfer of securities of a listed company
options.D: Non-payment of dividend by a listed company

answer_html:

Section 24(1)(a) assigns to SEBI only matters relating to issue and transfer of securities and non-payment of dividend by listed companies (or companies proposing to list). All other matters specifically provided in the Act - including matters relating to prospectus, return of allotment, and redemption of preference shares - are administered by the Central Government, Tribunal, or Registrar, as the case may be.

question_html: Under section 2(70), the definition of 'prospectus' has a 'means' part and an 'includes' part comprising four constituents in total. Which of the following is NOT one of those four constituents?

options.A: Any document described or issued as a prospectus
options.B: A shelf prospectus referred to in section 31, or a red herring prospectus referred to in section 32
options.C: Any document described or issued as an annual report of the company, containing the audited financial statements for the preceding financial year
options.D: Any notice, circular, advertisement or other document inviting offers from the public for the subscription or purchase of any securities of a body corporate

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Any document described or issued as an annual report of the company, containing the audited financial statements for the preceding financial year

Section 2(70) defines 'prospectus' to mean any document described or issued as a prospectus, and to include a red herring prospectus (section 32), a shelf prospectus (section 31), or any notice, circular, advertisement or other document inviting offers from the public for subscription or purchase of securities (the 'deemed prospectus' limb). An annual report containing audited financial statements is not one of these four constituents.

question_html: Under section 25(2), an allotment or agreement to allot securities is presumed to have been made with a view to offering them to the public if which of the following conditions is fulfilled?

options.A: The allottee is a company incorporated outside India, regardless of the timing of any subsequent offer to the public
options.B: The securities allotted represent more than 50% of the company's total paid-up share capital, regardless of the timing of any subsequent offer to the public
options.C: The allotment was approved by an ordinary (rather than a special) resolution of the company's members
options.D: The securities are offered to the public within six months of the allotment, or the full consideration for the securities has not been received by the company at the date the offer to the public is made

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The securities are offered to the public within six months of the allotment, or the full consideration for the securities has not been received by the company at the date the offer to the public is made

Section 25(2) presumes an intent to offer to the public where either: (a) the securities are offered to the public within six months of allotment, or (b) full consideration has not been received by the company at the date of the offer to the public. If either condition is met, the document by which the offer is made is deemed to be a prospectus under section 25(1).

question_html: What principle was established in Re, South of England Natural Gas and Petroleum Co. Ltd, where a document offering shares for subscription and headed 'For Private Circulation Only' was circulated to members of a limited class of gas companies?

options.A: A document headed 'For Private Circulation Only' can never be treated as a prospectus, however widely it is in fact circulated, since the heading itself is conclusive of the issuer's intent
options.B: Even though the offer was made only to a limited class of persons, it was nonetheless an offer to the public, since those persons from the limited class were themselves 'the public'; the document was therefore a prospectus and had to contain the particulars required by the Act
options.C: The offer was held not to be a prospectus because it was circulated to fewer than fifty persons in total, which is below the statutory threshold for a public offer
options.D: The offer was held to be a prospectus only because the recipients later resold their shares to outsiders, and not because of the manner of the original circulation

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Even though the offer was made only to a limited class of persons, it was nonetheless an offer to the public, since those persons from the limited class were themselves 'the public'; the document was therefore a prospectus and had to contain the particulars required by the Act

In Re, South of England Natural Gas and Petroleum Co. Ltd, it was held that circulating a document marked 'For Private Circulation Only' to members of a limited class was still an offer to the public - the term 'public' is not restricted to the public at large, and a limited class can itself constitute 'the public'. The document was therefore held to be a prospectus.

question_html: What did Nash v. Lynde establish regarding whether a single private communication, marked 'strictly private and confidential', constitutes an 'issue' of a prospectus to the public?

options.A: A single private communication always constitutes a valid issue to the public, regardless of how confidential or restricted its circulation may be
options.B: The term 'issue' requires the document to be circulated to at least one hundred persons simultaneously, failing which it can never be treated as an issue
options.C: The term 'issue' is not satisfied by a single private communication; there must be some measure of publicity, however modest, for a document to be construed as an issue attracting the Act's provisions relating to prospectus
options.D: Nash v. Lynde held that any document that omits material facts automatically becomes an 'issue' to the public, irrespective of its confidentiality marking or circulation

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The term 'issue' is not satisfied by a single private communication; there must be some measure of publicity, however modest, for a document to be construed as an issue attracting the Act's provisions relating to prospectus

In Nash v. Lynde, Nash applied for shares based on a document marked 'strictly private and confidential', sent to him by the company's managing director; his suit for compensation for omissions was dismissed. Viscount Sumner's dictum established that a private communication, not being 'open', does not constitute an 'issue' to the public - some measure of publicity is required.

question_html: In Smith v. Chadwick, a prospectus stated that the 'present value of turnover is £1 million sterling per annum'. What principle did the court apply in holding this to be a misleading statement?

options.A: A statement is misleading only if it is proved to be false under every possible interpretation that could be given to it, with no scope for partial ambiguity
options.B: The court held that turnover figures can never form the basis of a misleading-statement claim, since turnover is inherently a matter of professional opinion
options.C: Where a statement is capable of bearing more than one meaning, and the directors knew that one of those possible meanings was false to their knowledge, the statement is considered to be misleading
options.D: The statement was held misleading solely because it was expressed in a foreign currency rather than in Indian rupees

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Where a statement is capable of bearing more than one meaning, and the directors knew that one of those possible meanings was false to their knowledge, the statement is considered to be misleading

In Smith v. Chadwick, the statement about turnover was true only if production capacity were meant, but untrue if actual production/utilisation levels were meant. The court held that where a statement the directors know may bear multiple meanings, and one such meaning is false to their knowledge, this amounts to a misleading statement.

question_html:
Coastal Ceramics Limited allots 40,000 equity shares to Zenway Capital Advisors Pvt Ltd, with the understanding that Zenway would in turn offer those shares for sale to the public. Four months after the allotment to Zenway, Zenway issues a circular offering the shares to the public for subscription. At the time this circular is issued, Coastal Ceramics has already received the full consideration for the shares from Zenway. The circular issued by Zenway is signed, on behalf of Coastal Ceramics, by two of its directors, and states the net amount received as consideration and the time and place at which the underlying allotment contract may be inspected.

Is the circular issued by Zenway Capital Advisors Pvt Ltd, offering the Coastal Ceramics shares to the public four months after allotment, deemed to be a prospectus under section 25?

options.A: No - since Coastal Ceramics had already received full consideration for the shares before the circular was issued, the presumption of a view to offer to the public under section 25 is automatically rebutted
options.B: No - a deemed prospectus can only arise where the original allottee is a natural person, and never where the allottee is itself a company such as Zenway
options.C: Yes - since the shares were offered to the public within six months of the allotment, the allotment is presumed under section 25(2)(a) to have been made with a view to their being offered for sale to the public, and the circular is deemed to be a prospectus issued by Coastal Ceramics
options.D: Yes, but only if the circular is issued within thirty days (rather than six months) of the original allotment

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - since the shares were offered to the public within six months of the allotment, the allotment is presumed under section 25(2)(a) to have been made with a view to their being offered for sale to the public, and the circular is deemed to be a prospectus issued by Coastal Ceramics

Section 25(1) deems any document offering securities for sale, allotted with a view to public sale, to be a prospectus. Section 25(2)(a) presumes such a 'view' where the securities are offered to the public within six months of allotment - here, the four-month gap triggers this presumption, regardless of whether full consideration was received (that is an alternative, independent trigger under section 25(2)(b), not a condition that must also be absent).

Can Mr. Farooq, having suffered loss due to the omissions in the memorandum sent to him personally by Mr. Devraj, successfully invoke the Act's provisions relating to liability for prospectus omissions?

Correct answer: (B) No - following the principle in Nash v. Lynde, a single private communication marked 'strictly private and confidential', sent to one individual, does not constitute an 'issue' to the public and therefore does not amount to a prospectus attracting the Act's provisions

Per Nash v. Lynde, a single private communication (however material its omissions) is not open to the public and does not constitute an 'issue' - there must be some measure of publicity, however modest, for the document to be treated as a prospectus attracting liability under the Act.

topic_text: Private Placement - Consequence of Non-Compliant Offer Being Deemed a Public Offer
exam_applicability: Applicable for the May 2027 and onward CA Inter examinations, per the ICAI Study Material for Paper 2: Corporate and Other Laws (relevant for May, 2027 and onward examinations), revised on the basis of legislative developments made up till 30th June, 2026. Coverage includes Chapter III of the Companies Act, 2013 (sections 23 to 42) and the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014: public offer and private placement modes of issue under section 23, the meaning of 'securities' under section 2(81), the SEBI/Central Government division of regulatory jurisdiction under section 24, the meaning of 'prospectus' under section 2(70) and deemed prospectus under section 25 (including the presumption of intent to offer to the public, additional matters to be stated, and signing requirements), judicial principles on the meaning of 'public' and 'issue' (Re South of England Natural Gas and Petroleum Co. Ltd, Nash v. Lynde, SEBI v Kunnamkulam Paper Mills Ltd), matters to be stated in a prospectus and its filing/ validity under section 26, variation in terms of contract or objects stated in the prospectus under section 27, offer of sale of shares by certain members under section 28, dematerialised issue of securities under section 29, advertisement of prospectus under section 30, shelf prospectus under section 31, red herring prospectus under section 32, abridged prospectus under section 33, mis-statements in prospectus and the leading cases thereon (Henderson v. Lacon, Rex v. Kylsant, Smith v. Chadwick), remedies of rescission and damages for misrepresentation, civil liability under section 35 and criminal liability under section 34 for mis-statements, damages for deceit (Peek v. Gurney), punishment for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money under section 36, action by affected persons under section 37, punishment for personation for acquisition of securities under section 38, punishment for fraud under section 447, allotment of securities under section 39 (minimum subscription, application money, return of allotment), securities to be dealt with in stock exchanges and payment of underwriting commission under section 40, global depository receipts under section 41, and private placement of securities under section 42.
